papers.title: Distinguishing Initial-Condition and Model Error Using Machine-Learning Weather Models
papers.abstract: Gated and ungated optimizations evaluated in GraphCast and Pangu-Weather. The first panel (upper-left) shows the mean over the 36 dates; remaining panels show first-of-month 12 UTC optimization descents from January-November 2017. The y-axis metric is the summed day 1-10 Z500 RMSE verified against ERA5, expressed as percent change from each model's date-matched control. The gated arm optimizes the initial conditions jointly with a LoRA weight correction; its GraphCast curve uses the initial conditions alone (LoRA removed), the same state Pangu receives. Stars and diamonds mark the lowest Pangu errors in the 5- and 10-day windows, respectively. Percentages above each panel show the best Pangu improvement relative to control for gated (green) and ungated (red) optimization. Ungated outperforms gated on half of dates when stopped early. Gating does not guarantee a better Pangu performance, but it does produce more comparable GraphCast and Pangu-Weather improvements on all 36 cases.

papers.title: Shifts in Rossby wave regimes via the change of group velocity with zonal jets
papers.abstract: Evidences show it is questionable to use the trends in Rossby wave phase speed (Cpx) to interpret the relation between the changes of extreme events and westerly jets. We propose, by using 70 years (1954-2023) of ERA5 reanalysis, that the trends in extremes are associated with the shifts of Rossby wave regimes, via the westerly-induced changes in Rossby wave group velocity (Cgx), which are two to three times larger than those in Cpx. We find significant deceleration in the subtropics and polar regions, alongside a salient midlatitude acceleration, of Rossby wave Cgx, especially over the East Asia-Pacific-North America and North Atlantic-Europe sectors. These changes induce robust shifts in spatiotemporal regimes of Rossby waves, from the transient synoptic-scale regime toward the quasi-stationary planetary-scale wave regime where Cgx decelerates, and vice versa. The CESM2 Large Ensemble confirms that the observed pattern over the Eurasia-Pacific-North America sector is a forced response to external forcing, while uncertainties remain over the polar regions and the North Atlantic. We suggest that westerly trends may reshape the regimes of extratropical Rossby wave activity and extreme weather events through the changes in group velocity rather than phase speed of Rossby waves.

papers.title: Evaluating the prediction of subgrid eddy kinetic energy from a machine learning model
papers.abstract: Global climate model resolution is still too coarse to fully resolve mesoscale processes, therefore subgrid closures are required to approximate the feedback of eddies onto the resolved flow. With high-resolution datasets now readily available, there has been a rapid growth in the use of machine learning to develop new eddy closures that could help reduce model biases and uncertainty. In this work we employ an offline learning approach with a convolutional neural network to predict subgrid eddy kinetic energy ($KE_e$), laying the initial groundwork for a machine-learned scale-aware GEOMETRIC eddy closure for the UK's Earth System Model. We address the question of whether global parameterizations are needed or if regional closures are sufficient by evaluating a number of neural network models through region and feature ablation experiments. ML parameterization models generalize to unseen regions when their training data share similar feature and target distributions with those regions. Models that fail to generalize incur distributional shift, or employ different filtering scales for the true eddy kinetic energy field. When holding out features, there is improvement among the generalizable ML models, with some feature spaces leading to improvements in some regions but degrading performance in others. Generally, power spectral density of $KE_e$ tend to diverge at small scales, though some feature spaces are able to minimize this divergence. Overall, the best performing model trained on all regions achieves time-mean and anomaly R2 scores of R2$\approx 0.95$ and R2$\approx 0.8 - 0.9$, respectively.

papers.title: Temporary gas turbines powering a US AI data center created a cross-state air pollution hotspot
papers.abstract: Data centers increasingly use on-site gas turbines that regulators can treat as temporary. Two satellites show the fleet powering SpaceXAI's Colossus 2 raised local nitrogen dioxide columns by about half as it expanded, the most anomalous increase among 656 urban locations nationwide since 2020. Mississippi authorized the fleet, but two-thirds of the hotspot's 116,000 mostly Black residents live in Tennessee, and the hotspot contains no regulatory nitrogen dioxide monitor. The fleet causes an estimated four premature deaths yearly, valued at $49 million, over 80% outside Mississippi and nearly all from units without selective catalytic reduction. On new turbines, this control's benefits exceed costs over the service life, but not over temporary stays or for in-state damages alone. Standards following the equipment could recover these benefits.

papers.title: A plea for Miles' approach to wind-wave interaction
papers.abstract: Although the phenomenon of wave growth under the effect of wind still holds many open questions, the approach initiated by Miles [1] is a cornerstone of the current comprehension. This theory is based on physical arguments, keeping phenomenological input to a minimum, but it can be perceived as intimidating, especially in view of concrete applications. Here we argue that Miles' results can be summarised in terms of a simple functional form, which provides an easy-to-use expression to work with. We furthermore show that Miles' predictions do not, as is often stated, underestimate growth rates, once the presence of a whole wave spectrum is accounted for. Finally, we illustrate that the generalisation of Miles' original result to complex hydrodynamic situations can be quite straightforward. Our hands-on summary should make it heretofore very easy to exploit Miles' approach in practice.

papers.title: Comparing the dynamics of idealized squall lines between NWP and LES models
papers.abstract: Mesoscale convective systems, such as squall lines, produce large amounts of rainfall but remain challenging to forecast. We intercompare two atmospheric models, namely ICON (ICOsahedral Non-hydrostatic) and MicroHH, to investigate how a simulated squall line depends on the model formulation. ICON is a Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) model, which traditionally aims for accurate weather forecasts, whereas MicroHH is typically used to study physical processes with Large-Eddy Simulations (LES). These different purposes resulted in different designs, mainly because ICON solves the compressible equations on a triangular grid, while MicroHH solves the anelastic equations on a regular grid. With increasing computer power, the applications of these models converge, raising the question of whether the model results also converge. We investigated an idealized squall line with the same case setup in both models, including grid spacing, domain size, boundary conditions, and microphysics scheme. The models simulate the same squall-line structure and circulation pattern. Furthermore, the mean vertical wind and upward mass and humidity fluxes differ less than 5% averaged over the cloud layer at 500 m grid spacing. In contrast, ICON produces less surface precipitation than MicroHH and has higher maximum vertical velocities across grid spacings. At 500 m grid spacing, inter model differences are controlled by the advection scheme and the formulation of moist thermodynamics while differences in the turbulent formulation are less relevant. The quantitative differences between the models across grid spacings highlight that the details of model physics and numerics are at least as important as the grid spacing.

papers.title: Unmasking Compensating Errors in Numerical Weather Models: A Process-Additive Neural Network Approach
papers.abstract: This work introduces a Process Additive Neural Network (PANN) framework to disentangle compensating biases in atmospheric models, where errors in different physical processes can offset each other and obscure their origins. Using a single-column model, each PANN branch represents the tendency error associated with a separate physical process, and the summed branch outputs approximate the total error relative to a reference tendency. Once trained successfully, the branch outputs are expected to provide process-level error attributions and, when averaged, estimates of process-level bias. Initial experiments focus on cloud-related processes in OpenIFS SCM case studies, where cloud and convection tendencies are strongly coupled and compensation is difficult to diagnose using standard approaches. The aim is not to replace human interpretation of physical processes, but to extend it to regimes where model complexity, process interaction, and compensating errors make direct diagnosis difficult. By providing a physically structured form of machine-learning interpretability, PANN can help connect complex model behaviour with process-level explanations. This work supports both improved understanding of compensating errors and the development of more physically consistent weather and climate models.
